# Published errors — errors in published health metadata

*Generated by `report.py` from `results/summary.json` on
2026-09-30T14:32:16+00:00. Do not hand-edit: regenerate.*

## Headline

> **69.1% of published health dataset records violate the application profile they claim to conform to. 96.3% of the defects found are structurally preventable at entry — a form generated from the profile could not have submitted them.**

Against the profile's **published SHACL file alone**, the violation rate is 37.4% (95% CI 32.6–42.4%). Adding the constraints the profile states in prose but does not ship as SHACL takes it to 69.1% (CI 64.2–73.6%). The gap between those two numbers is itself a finding, and it is discussed below.

Of 77 source catalogues in the sample, 23 had no record with a violation. This is not a story about a careless portal — it is a story about a pipeline with no gate.

## Sample

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | data.europa.eu public SPARQL endpoint |
| Population | dataset records with `dcat:theme` = EU data-theme `HEAL` |
| Population size | 33,228 records in 77 source catalogues |
| Sample size | **n = 372** |
| Design | stratified by source catalogue; near-proportional allocation with a floor of 2 and a cap of 40 per stratum |
| Draw | uniform without replacement inside each stratum, seed `20260827` |
| Frame built | 2026-08-27T15:57:03+00:00 |
| Records that failed to parse | 0 |

The floor is there so the result speaks about the ecosystem rather than about
whichever portal happens to be largest; the cap is there so no single portal can
drive the headline. Both distortions are undone by Horvitz–Thompson weights for
the population estimate, and the unweighted figure is reported alongside.

| Estimator | records with a violation (L1+L2) |
|---|---:|
| Sample proportion | 69.1% |
| Population-weighted (H–T) | 78.7% |
| Equal weight per catalogue | 55.3% |

The spread between them is the design showing through, and it is worth reading
rather than averaging away. Weighting back to the population *raises* the rate to
78.7%, because the largest catalogues are the
ones the cap held back. Weighting every catalogue equally *lowers* it to
55.3%, because many small catalogues are
clean. Whichever way the sample is weighted, most published records violate the
profile; the headline uses the plain sample proportion, which sits between the
two.

## What was validated against what

Three layers, kept separate on purpose.

| Layer | Shapes | Preventable at entry? |
|---|---|---|
| **L1** | DCAT-AP 3.0.1 SHACL, exactly as SEMIC publishes it (`dcat-ap-SHACL.ttl`, tag `3.0.1`, commit `21f43cee`) | yes |
| **L2** | constraints DCAT-AP 3.0.1 states in prose but does **not** express in SHACL: membership of the EU authority tables its "controlled vocabularies that MUST be used" table names — `dct:accrualPeriodicity`, `dct:format`, `adms:status`, `dcatap:availability`, `dct:language`, `dcat:mediaType`; plus the three `sh:uniqueLang` constraints the official Health-RI formalisation of HealthDCAT-AP applies (`dct:title`, `dct:description`, `adms:versionNotes`); plus `sh:minLength 1` on the two mandatory literals, because `sh:minCount` is satisfied by `dct:title ""` and no published profile adds it | yes |
| **L3** | defects no SHACL profile can express: a distribution link that does not resolve; a record whose last modification contradicts its own declared `dct:accrualPeriodicity`; a placeholder value that is structurally perfect and semantically empty | **no** |

L3 exists to keep the second headline honest. Every constraint a SHACL profile
*can* state is, by construction, one a shape-driven form can enforce before
submission — so a taxonomy built only from SHACL results would report 100%
preventable and would mean nothing. The preventable share is only interesting
measured against a defect inventory that also contains things entry-time
validation cannot fix.

That cuts both ways, and it is the main caveat on the second number: the
preventable share moves with how many L3 checks are in the denominator. Three
were implemented. A study that checked more kinds of semantic decay would report
a lower share; one that checked none would report 100%.

### Every defect kind, and which side of the split it falls on

The whole weight of the second headline rests on this mapping, so it is set out
in full rather than asserted. The last column marks the kinds named directly in
the experiment's own definition of preventable-at-entry — *missing required
property, wrong datatype, value outside `sh:in`, malformed IRI, missing language
tag*.

| Layer | Constraint | Defect class | Bucket | Named in the definition | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|---:|
| L2 | `sh:in` | value outside the mandated vocabulary | **preventable** | yes | 594 |
| L1 | `sh:datatype` | wrong datatype | **preventable** | yes | 330 |
| L1 | `sh:class` | wrong class for a described node | **preventable** | no | 136 |
| L1 | `sh:nodeKind` | wrong node kind / malformed IRI | **preventable** | yes | 136 |
| L1 | `sh:maxCount` | cardinality exceeded | **preventable** | no | 46 |
| L1 | `sh:minCount` | missing required property | **preventable** | yes | 40 |
| L3 | (no SHACL constraint can express it) | not refreshed at its own declared frequency | not preventable | n/a | 34 |
| L2 | `sh:minLength` | mandatory property present but empty | **preventable** | no | 18 |
| L2 | `sh:pattern` | malformed value | **preventable** | yes | 17 |
| L3 | (no SHACL constraint can express it) | distribution link does not resolve | not preventable | n/a | 13 |
| L3 | (no SHACL constraint can express it) | record carries an IRI a conformant Turtle parser must reject | not preventable | n/a | 2 |
| L3 | (no SHACL constraint can express it) | placeholder value, structurally valid | not preventable | n/a | 1 |

Three preventable kinds are ours rather than the definition's, and they are
marked `no` above: `sh:maxCount` (a form generated from the shape emits one
field, so it cannot over-supply), `sh:class` on a node **the record itself
describes** (the form knows the class of the node it is building — `sh:class` on
a node the record merely *references* is not counted at all, see "not
assessable"), and `sh:minLength`. Excluding all three leaves
1117 defects, or
81.7%, that the definition names
outright. That is the floor under the second headline:

| Reading of "preventable at entry" | n | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| everything a SHACL shape can express (headline) | 1317 | 96.3% |
| per distinct defect site rather than per failed constraint | 406 | 89.0% |
| only the kinds the definition names outright (floor) | 1117 | 81.7% |

The three differ by 14.6
percentage points and none of them changes the conclusion.

### Two defects in the profile artefact itself

Found while building L1, and both worth reporting upstream independently of this
paper.

1. **`dcat-ap-SHACL.ttl` contains zero `sh:in` and zero `sh:pattern`.** The same
   document's prose carries a table headed *"controlled vocabularies that MUST be
   used"* and says of that class of requirement: *"Validation systems SHOULD
   produce errors."* No validator running the published shapes can produce those
   errors, because the published shapes do not encode them. That gap is the
   entire distance between the L1 and the L1+L2 numbers.
2. **`dcat:DataServiceShape` links 2
   property shapes that do not exist.** `sh:property` points at two IRIs with no
   triples anywhere in the file, so `dcat:DataServiceShape` states two
   constraints that say nothing. A profile that cannot round-trip through its own
   document is a profile nobody validated. They were dropped before validation;
   an empty property shape constrains nothing, so dropping them cannot hide a
   violation, and `conformance.py` checks that rather than asserting it — the
   same deliberately-violating `dcat:DataService` gets the same four results
   under the shapes as published and under the de-dangled shapes.

| bucket | defects | share |
|---|---:|---:|
| **preventable at entry** | 1317 | 96.3% |
| **not preventable at entry** | 50 | 3.7% |

One underlying mistake can raise more than one result: the generated DCAT-AP
shapes put each constraint in its own property shape, so a literal where an IRI
is required comes back as both `sh:class` and `sh:nodeKind`. Counting distinct
(record, focus class, path) **sites** instead of failed constraints gives
456 sites, of which 89.0%
are preventable. That is the conservative reading of the second headline: on the
per-constraint unit it is 96.3%, on the per-site
unit 89.0%. Both are reported; neither changes
the picture.

### Set aside: not assessable

**1,175** constraint results were discarded as *not
assessable*: they turn on the `rdf:type` of a node nobody publishes a type for.
They may or may not be real. Charging them to a publisher would be wrong, so they
are reported and dropped.

| Path | Constraint | n |
|---|---|---:|
| `dcat:theme` | `sh:class` | 380 |
| `dct:license` | `sh:class` | 194 |
| `dct:format` | `sh:class` | 180 |
| `spdx:algorithm` | `sh:class` | 115 |
| `dcat:mediaType` | `sh:class` | 50 |
| `dct:spatial` | `sh:class` | 46 |
| `dcat:accessService` | `sh:class` | 43 |
| `dcat:landingPage` | `sh:class` | 43 |
| `dct:conformsTo` | `sh:class` | 31 |
| `foaf:page` | `sh:class` | 22 |
| `dcatap:availability` | `sh:class` | 19 |
| `dcat:compressFormat` | `sh:class` | 11 |

It is one structural cause, and it is worth stating because it is another way the
post-hoc gate fails in practice. DCAT-AP constrains `dct:license`, `dct:format`,
`dcat:landingPage` and `spdx:algorithm` with `sh:class`, and the values are
ordinary web URLs — a Creative Commons deed, an IANA media-type page — that carry
no `rdf:type` anywhere. `sh:class` cannot be satisfied against them unless
someone supplies the missing typing, so a validator run over a real record
produces these results *every time, for every record* — a mean of
3.2 per record here, against a median of
2 real defects. 46.2%
of everything the validator hands an operator is this. A report that is nearly
half unfixable noise is a report nobody reads twice. This is what a gate looks
like when it has been left switched on and pointed at nothing.

The type assertions the aggregator's own store does publish were loaded first, so
this table is what remains after that. Loading them also drags the EU authority
concepts themselves into the validator's target set, which raised a further
5,186 results about the *vocabularies* rather than
about any record; those are out of scope and are not counted anywhere.

### What is actually in those fields

Four properties carry most of the sample's defects. This is what their values
look like — categorised by namespace or datatype only, never by value, so
nothing here identifies a publisher.

| Path | Value shape | n | share |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `adms:status` | IRI from the superseded purl.org/adms/status vocabulary | 187 | 95.9% |
| `adms:status` | IRI from a different EU authority table | 8 | 4.1% |
| `dcat:byteSize` | plain literal, no datatype | 112 | 46.1% |
| `dcat:byteSize` | typed xsd:integer | 104 | 42.8% |
| `dcat:byteSize` | typed xsd:nonNegativeInteger | 27 | 11.1% |
| `dcat:mediaType` | IRI from the mandated IANA media-type registry | 731 | 97.7% |
| `dcat:mediaType` | plain literal where the profile mandates an IRI | 16 | 2.1% |
| `dcat:mediaType` | IRI from the EU File Type table that dct:format mandates | 1 | 0.1% |
| `dct:format` | IRI from the mandated EU File Type table | 813 | 72.1% |
| `dct:format` | IRI from outside any mandated vocabulary | 246 | 21.8% |
| `dct:format` | plain literal where the profile mandates an IRI | 62 | 5.5% |
| `dct:format` | IRI from the IANA registry that dcat:mediaType mandates | 7 | 0.6% |

Read down that table and the defects stop looking like carelessness.

`adms:status` is the clearest case: **not one value in the sample** uses the
authority table DCAT-AP 3.0.1 mandates. They are on `purl.org/adms/status`, the
vocabulary the earlier revision of the profile specified, or on a neighbouring
EU table. This is a vocabulary migration that nothing forced anybody through —
there is no gate that would have said "that table moved".

`dcat:byteSize` is the second: the required datatype is `xsd:nonNegativeInteger`
and most values are an untyped literal or a plain `xsd:integer`. No human
notices that by eye. A generated form emits the datatype the shape declares, by
construction, and cannot get it wrong.

`dct:format` and `dcat:mediaType` are the third, and they refute a tempting
story. The two properties are mandated to draw on *different* registries — the
EU File Type table and the IANA media-type registry — and it is natural to
assume the errors are the two being swapped. They are not: swapped values are a
rounding error in this sample. What is actually there is a value from neither
registry, or a bare literal like `CSV` where an IRI is required. The mistake is
not confusion between two vocabularies. It is the absence of any mechanism that
asks a vocabulary for a value at all.

Per-catalogue violation rate, over 77 catalogues. Deliberately
reported as a five-number summary and never as a table of names.

| | min | Q1 | median | Q3 | max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| L1 only | 0.0% | 0.0% | 0.0% | 50.0% | 100.0% |
| L1 + L2 | 0.0% | 0.0% | 59.4% | 100.0% | 100.0% |

23 of 77 catalogues

## Descriptive findings, not scored as defects

| | n | share of sample |
|---|---:|---:|
| Records whose `dct:title` carries no language tag at all | 59 | 15.9% |
| Records with no `dct:description` reaching the aggregator | 2 | 0.5% |
| Records with at least one L3 (not preventable) defect | 48 | 12.9% |

DCAT-AP does not *require* a language tag on `dct:title`, so an untagged title is
not a violation. It is still the thing that stops a record being reusable outside
its own country, and it is exactly what an entry-time form with a language-aware
literal widget makes hard to get wrong.

And the ecosystem clearly feels the gap: **38,821** literals
in the sample (297 of 372 records) are machine
translations the aggregator produced after the fact, tagged with a BCP-47
`-t-…-t0-mt…` transform extension. All were removed before validation. Post-hoc
translation of a monolingual record is the same move as post-hoc validation of an
invalid one: repair downstream, because nothing upstream asked.

## Method

1. `harvest.py frame` — one SPARQL query for per-catalogue HEAL counts, then one
   per catalogue for its dataset IRIs.
2. `harvest.py sample` — stratified draw, fixed seed.
3. `harvest.py fetch` — two anchored `CONSTRUCT` queries per record.
4. `harvest.py types` — `rdf:type` of the external IRIs the records reference.
5. `ontology.py` — `rdfs:subClassOf` axioms from the range vocabularies.
6. `vocab_shapes.py` — fetch the EU authority tables and emit L2 as SHACL.
7. `linkcheck.py` — one `HEAD` per record against the first `dcat:accessURL`.
8. `validate.py` — clean, validate, classify, write `summary.json`.
9. `report.py` — render this file.

**Engine: @kanzo-tech/rudof-wasm@0.3.10** (wasm), on Node
v23.9.0, loaded exactly as `src/engine/RudofEngine.ts` loads it.
This is the engine the library ships and the engine the form runs on commit, so
it is the engine whose verdict the claim is about. rdflib
7.6.0 parses, cleans and re-serializes the records; it is an
RDF toolkit, not a SHACL engine, and decides nothing about conformance.

An earlier round of this experiment ran the whole corpus through a second SHACL
implementation as well and diffed the two reports defect by defect. That
instrument did its job — it found two real rudof defects, a validation bypass in
which the parser silently discarded triples with malformed IRIs, and
`sh:targetClass` not selecting through the `rdfs:subClassOf` closure — and both
are fixed in the version above. It is not in the pipeline any more, and no
number here depends on one. What replaced it needs no second engine:
`conformance.py` probes every construct these shapes use against a case whose
answer the specification's own words decide, and `version_delta.py` re-runs the
identical staged corpus through the previous release so that "the numbers moved
because the engine got stricter" is measured rather than argued.

**2 record(s) the parser refused.** rudof
0.3.10 raises on an IRI it will not accept rather than
dropping the triple. Two records in this corpus carry one, so no validator can
say anything about them; they are counted as an L3 defect
(`UnparseableRecord`) rather than as conformant, because a record no validator
can read has not passed anything. Over the
370 records it did read, rudof loaded
93395 of the 93395
triples staged for it — a difference of
0.

Before validation each record graph is cleaned of things the aggregator added
rather than the publisher: `dqv` quality annotations, and machine-translated
literals (BCP-47 `-t-…-t0-mt…` transform tags).

## Threats to validity

**This is not a uniform random sample, and the headline CI is not a population
CI.** 372 records were drawn from 33,228, a sampling fraction of
1.12%. Because of the floor and the cap, a
record's chance of being drawn varies by a factor of
191 between strata — from
0.52% in the largest catalogue to
100% in the
17 catalogues small enough that the floor of
2 took all of them. 37 strata sit at
the floor, 1 at the cap. The weighted design effect is
1.43, so the 372 records carry about as much
information as 260 drawn uniformly.

The consequence matters for how the headline is quoted. The interval beside the
sample proportion (69.1%, CI 64.2–73.6%) is a
binomial interval, and it is correct **for the sample proportion only** — it is
not an interval for the population. The population estimate is the
Horvitz–Thompson one, 78.7%, and its
design-corrected interval is
75.4–82.0%. Both are
reported throughout; neither is anywhere near a rate that would make the claim
marginal. What the design *cannot* support is a statement about any single
catalogue: at the floor, a stratum contributes 2 records, and
2 records say nothing about a portal. That is a limitation, and
it is also the point — the experiment is built so that it cannot make that
statement even by accident.

**The aggregator is in the path.** Records were read from the EU aggregator, not
from each publisher's own endpoint. The aggregator harvests, normalises and
re-serialises; some of what is measured here may have been introduced or repaired
in that step rather than authored. The correct reading of this experiment is
therefore *"the record as a consumer receives it"*, not *"the record as a
publisher wrote it"* — and that is the reading the claim needs anyway, because
the argument is that **no** stage of the chain has an entry-time gate. It does
mean no defect here can be attributed to any particular actor, which is also why
none is.

**Harvest scope decides some results.** A `sh:class` constraint on an IRI nobody
publishes a type for cannot be evaluated. Those results are counted separately
(1,175 of them) and excluded. An
earlier version of the harvest used `DESCRIBE`, which on this Virtuoso returns a
blank node's identity but not its properties; that made every record look as
though it had an empty `dcat:contactPoint` and `dct:provenance`. The published
harvester uses anchored `CONSTRUCT`s instead. It is worth stating plainly that
the first run of this experiment produced a much worse — and wrong — number.
1 record(s) of 372 lost the second harvest query to
a server timeout and were validated without it.

**L1 is a moving target.** DCAT-AP 3.0.1 was released in June 2026. Records
harvested before then were authored against 2.1.1 or 3.0.0. Constraints that
tightened between releases are charged here to records that predate them.

**L2 is our construction.** DCAT-AP 3.0.1 ships no `sh:in` and no `sh:pattern` at
all, so authority-table conformance had to be written as shapes for this study.
It was kept to the properties the specification puts in its *"controlled
vocabularies that MUST be used"* table — of which its own text says "Validation
systems SHOULD produce errors" — and nothing weaker is scored: `dct:accessRights`
is RECOMMENDED and `dct:type` on a Dataset is MAY, so neither is counted, even
though both are frequently off-vocabulary in the sample. `dcat:theme` is excluded
as circular: the sample is *defined* by carrying the `HEAL` theme. Two L2 checks
are namespace patterns rather than enumerations (`dct:language`,
`dcat:mediaType`), which accept a well-formed IRI in the right namespace even
when the concept does not exist — so L2 under-counts there. The two
`sh:minLength 1` constraints are ours outright: no published DCAT-AP or
HealthDCAT-AP shape has one, which is why `dct:title ""` conforms to every
validator in the ecosystem while carrying no title. For the record, the three
`sh:uniqueLang` constraints fired
0 times in this
sample: they are in L2 because the health profile applies them, not because they
carry the result.

**L3 is not exhaustive and not stable.** Link status was probed once, with one
`HEAD` per record. Re-running on another day will give a slightly different L3
count. Only `gone` (404/410), `dns_fail` and `conn_fail` are counted as dead —
13 of 372 records. Everything else is
recorded and *not* counted, deliberately: a portal that refuses `HEAD` from an
unknown client is not a broken link, and neither is a certificate that this
Python trust store rejects and a browser might not.

| link status | n |
|---|---:|
| `ok` | 233 |
| `tls_fail` | 58 |
| `no_access_url` | 44 |
| `blocked` | 14 |
| `gone` | 12 |
| `http_400` | 3 |
| `server_error` | 3 |
| `timeout` | 2 |
| `dns_fail` | 1 |
| `http_302` | 1 |
| `unknown` | 1 |

**Theme HEAL is an aggregator classification.** Some records under it are health-
adjacent rather than health data, and health datasets whose publisher did not tag
them HEAL are outside the frame.

**The preventable share depends on the inventory** — see the note under
"What was validated against what". It is the softer of the two headline numbers.

## Licence and ethics

data.europa.eu's legal notice waives rights in portal **metadata** under CC0 1.0,
so redistribution would be permitted. The harvested records are nonetheless
**not** committed. Two reasons, and the licence is neither of them:

1. The records contain personal data. `dcat:contactPoint` routinely carries a
   named individual's name, telephone and e-mail. The portal's own legal notice
   flags this. Mirroring it into a public git repository indefinitely is not
   something CC0 makes appropriate.
2. A committed corpus keyed by record, next to a per-record defect count, is the
   leaderboard this experiment undertook not to publish.

What is committed instead: the harvest scripts, the sampling parameters and
stratum sizes (`data/sample-frame.json`), the shapes of all three layers, and a
checksum manifest (`data/manifest.csv`) giving each record IRI and the SHA-256 of
the exact graph that was validated. That is enough to re-harvest and verify
byte-for-byte. `data/ref-types.ttl` and `data/linkcheck.csv` are excluded on the
same reasoning — the first is in effect a roster of publisher agent IRIs, the
second a per-record verdict — and both are regenerated by the scripts.

`results/violations.csv` carries one row per defect under an opaque record label.
The label is a rank over the record's own defect signature, so recovering the
mapping requires the harvested graphs — which are not committed. `manifest.csv`
and `violations.csv` share no ordering information.

That is worth spelling out, because the first version of this experiment got it
wrong. It drew the label from a shuffle of the manifest order under a fixed
seed, and both halves of that were committed: the seed was a constant in
`validate.py`, the row order is `manifest.csv`. The mapping was invertible in
about eight lines of Python, which made this file a per-record defect count
keyed by dataset IRI and source catalogue — the leaderboard the experiment
undertook not to publish — while this section claimed the opposite. An
anonymisation scheme whose key material is committed beside the data is not an
anonymisation scheme. It is recorded here rather than quietly fixed, because
the failure mode is easy to repeat.

No portal, publisher or institution is named anywhere in this file or in any
figure derived from it, and no per-record excerpt appears. The finding is about
the absence of an entry-time gate in the process, and it is written to be read
aloud in a room containing the people who run these portals.
